record.paper_title: Stationary solutions of the axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov system: present status and open problems
record.original_question: Do the high-angular-momentum rotating toroidal Einstein-Vlasov solution sequences have a genuine thin-ring limiting solution whose matter distribution behaves like a Dirac-type ring, and can that limit be used analytically, as thin shells are used in spherical symmetry, to prove existence or compactness bounds for axially symmetric solutions?

evidence.quote: The thin-ring limit discussed in the section above has interesting properties of its own. As shown in [3] the limiting members of solution sequences approaching this limit appear to display a local conical geometry around the matter, reminiscent of cosmic strings.
Due to the near Dirac nature of the spatial matter distribution in this limit, proving existence of such solutions may be analytically tractable.
Perhaps a similar study is possible in the axially symmetric case by utilizing the Dirac nature of the thin ring solutions.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the stationary axially symmetric Einstein–Vlasov system, in which a collisionless ensemble of particles obeys the Vlasov equation on a stationary, axially symmetric Lorentzian spacetime $(M,g)$ whose metric is sourced via the Einstein equations $G_{\mu\nu}=8\pi T_{\mu\nu}$ by the energy–momentum tensor
$$T_{\mu\nu}(x)=\int_{P_x} f(x,p)\, p_\mu p_\nu \, \frac{d^3p}{\sqrt{-\det g}\,|p_t|},$$
where $f\ge 0$ is a non-negative phase-space distribution function supported on the future mass-shell. Assume the existence of one-parameter families of stationary toroidal solutions with non-vanishing total angular momentum $J$, parameterized so that, along the family, the spatial support of $f$ concentrates onto a circle (the "thin-ring" regime), with proper transverse radius tending to zero while $J$ stays bounded away from zero.

Address the following:

(a) Does there exist a genuine limiting object, i.e. a stationary axisymmetric solution of the Einstein–Vlasov system in a distributional or appropriately weak sense, in which the matter is supported on a one-dimensional ring and behaves as a Dirac-type measure transverse to that ring, obtained as a limit of such high–angular-momentum toroidal sequences?

(b) If such a thin-ring limiting solution exists, can it be used analytically — in analogy to the use of thin-shell solutions in the spherically symmetric Einstein–Vlasov system — to establish existence results, a priori bounds, or compactness for stationary axially symmetric Einstein–Vlasov solutions with non-zero angular momentum?
artifact.status_search_result: Numerical studies of toroidal Vlasov bodies in general relativity (Ames, Andréasson, Logg, Phys. Rev. D 99, 024012, 2019) document a thin-ring/cosmic-string limit and a black-hole limit for sequences of axisymmetric stationary Einstein–Vlasov solutions, but the existence of a genuine distributional thin-ring limit and its analytical use to prove existence/compactness for axially symmetric solutions is presented as an open problem in subsequent surveys; no proof appears to have been published.

status_evidence.title: Cosmic string and black hole limits of toroidal Vlasov bodies in general relativity
status_evidence.snippet: Numerical investigation of limits of a two-parameter family of stationary toroidal Einstein–Vlasov solutions with nonvanishing angular momentum, identifying a cosmic-string-like thin-ring limit.
status_evidence.claim: The thin-ring limit has been studied numerically, with conical/Dirac-source features observed, but a rigorous limiting solution and its analytical exploitation are not established.

status_evidence.title: Stationary solutions of the axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov system: present status and open problems
status_evidence.snippet: Survey listing thin-ring limit existence and its analytical use as open problems in the axially symmetric Einstein–Vlasov theory.
status_evidence.claim: The question of a genuine Dirac-type thin-ring limit and its use to prove existence/compactness in the axisymmetric setting remains open.
